text: Hannah had come to the storage unit only to sort through her late uncle's tools, a task she had postponed for two months. She pulled up the metal door, and the smell of cedar and motor oil rolled out. Halfway down the aisle, behind a stack of paint cans, she found a plywood crate stamped with her grandmother's maiden name. Inside, wrapped in newspaper from 1974, was a leather-bound ledger and a bundle of letters in a hand she recognized. She was surprised first by the weight of it, then by the dates, which placed the letters within a year of her own birth. She read the first page standing on the concrete floor with her phone's flashlight in her teeth. The letter named a man who was not her grandfather. Hannah sat down on an overturned bucket, genuinely shocked, and began to read more slowly, aware that a family story she had accepted without question for forty years had just rearranged itself around her like furniture moved in the dark.

Title: My landlord just told me the building is being sold and I was NOT expecting that

I've rented the same two-bedroom for nine years. Last week I got an email from the property manager saying the building had been sold and to expect a "transition meeting." I honestly thought I'd misread it. Rent was the one thing I thought was stable. The new owner is an LLC I've never heard of.

I was surprised by how fast it all moved. Nobody mentioned a sale when I renewed in the spring. The meeting is Thursday, and they haven't said whether the lease will be honored. My neighbor, who has been here longer than me, said she'd heard the same rumor twice and it turned out to be nothing, so I'm trying not to freak out.

Has anyone dealt with a sale of a rent-stabilized building? What questions should I ask? Do I need a tenant lawyer before Thursday, or is that overkill? I'm still in shock, to be honest. I keep thinking about the mail I'd have to forward and the boxes I'd have to find. Thanks in advance for any help.

Dear Dad,

I know you'll read this as me making a fuss, but I need you to hear it in writing before we talk on Sunday. Mum's ring was not in the box you gave me. I was surprised, and then I was properly shocked when I checked the inventory list you sent last spring and it wasn't on that either. I've been going back over the last few years trying to understand how it could have gone missing without anyone noticing.

I'm not accusing you of anything. I just want to know the sequence. Did the jeweler collect it? Did you sell it when things were tight after Mum's surgery? You don't have to answer yes or no to any of that, but please don't tell me again that the box was always like that. It wasn't.

I've also been surprised by how much this has hurt. I thought I'd feel relieved to have a list of things we can work through, but mostly I feel like I've been living in a house I didn't fully know.

Love,
Claire

Sat 14th. Was halfway through my second coffee when the noise from the garden made me drop the mug. Went outside in my socks and found the fence panel flat on the lawn, three neighbors standing at their back doors, and a deer, an actual deer, in the middle of my tomato bed looking at me. Nobody moved for a long moment. Then it stepped over the hydrangea and went through the gap toward the park. Mrs. Okafor from next door asked if I was all right. I said yes and then could not stop laughing, which made the dog bark at me. Called the council about the fence. Took photos of the tomato plants, which are mostly trampled. Found a hoof print in the soft soil by the rain barrel, the size of my palm. Made tea and sat on the back step with it going cold. Mrs. Okafor's grandson came over with a tape measure and a bag of carrots, and we spent an hour trying to work out how the thing had squeezed through a gap that small.

Teodor had been on the night shift for eleven years and knew the sounds of the warehouse the way other men knew their own breathing. At 2:14 the conveyor on line four stopped, which it had never done without a warning light, and in the sudden quiet he heard someone shout his name from the far end of the floor. He walked toward the voice past pallets stacked to the rafters. A supervisor he barely knew was kneeling beside a man in a grey hi-vis vest, who had not been on the schedule that night and whom Teodor had never seen before. Blood had soaked through the cuff of his sleeve. The new man's eyes were open and moving. Teodor pulled the first aid kit from the wall box and tore a bandage open with his teeth. Somewhere a radio was crackling with a dispatcher asking for the status of the loading bay. Teodor pressed down with both hands and counted, the way he had been taught in a classroom five years earlier, until the ambulance lights came sweeping across the high windows.
